title: Gas appliances that work with no electricity
keywords: light gas stove with a match
summary: In a power cut, a standing-pilot (millivolt) gas fireplace or heater, a standing-pilot tank water heater and the burners on top of a gas range can still work. Electronic-ignition furnaces and modern ovens can't, and you should assume a boiler can't either. Every one of them makes carbon monoxide, and the oven is never a room heater.

steps.text: Before you light anything, make sure there is no smell of gas, a battery CO alarm is working in the room and outside every sleeping area, and the appliance's outside vent is clear of snow (Health Canada CO). If you smell gas, stop and follow [Gas safety](#guides/safety_natural_gas).
steps.warn: A buried or blocked vent pushes exhaust back into the house. Clear snow from vents by hand or with a broom. Around the meter and regulator, use a broom not a shovel, and never kick or hit the meter to free ice (PERC safety guide, BC gas brochure).

steps.text: Work out which kind you have, using the checklist in the notes: look for a small flame that burns all the time (a standing pilot), a valve knob marked OFF, PILOT and ON, and whether the appliance has a power cord, plug or battery box.
Gas range: hold a lit match or long lighter next to a top burner, then turn its knob to LO (GE outage). Stay with it, and keep every burner either lit or off.
steps.warn: A knob left at LITE or any setting with no flame lets gas flow into the room (GE outage).

steps.text: Don't try to light a gas oven, an electronic-ignition furnace with a match, and treat a boiler the same unless its own label says otherwise. The oven's glow-bar igniter and gas valve need power to open (GE outage), and furnace makers say not to light the burner by hand (Goodman IO-359J, Lennox EL297UHV).
steps.warn: Never heat a room with the oven or the range-top burners (PERC safety guide).

steps.text: Standing-pilot fireplace or heater: if the pilot is lit, the wall switch, remote or millivolt thermostat still turns it on; the blower won't run (Travis 864 ST). Keep the glass in place and children away from it.

If a pilot is out, relight it only by the lighting instructions on the appliance's own label (for a water heater, with its tank full of water first, Manitoba Hydro meters), and only if you can reach the pilot and see whether it lights. Wait 5 minutes or more with the knob at OFF to clear any gas first, and stop if you smell gas (NRCan gas fireplaces, Travis 864 ST). Some fireplaces need the glass off to light the pilot: let it cool first and put it back before the main burner runs, and use the built-in igniter, not a match, if the maker says so (Travis 864 ST).
steps.warn: If a pilot won't light or keeps going out, leave it off: don't take the valve or pilot apart (PERC safety guide).

notes:
## What needs power and what doesn't

| Appliance | Works with no power? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Gas fireplace, insert or heater with a standing pilot (millivolt) | Yes, except the blower | The pilot heats a thermopile that makes the small current the gas valve and wall switch use (Travis 864 ST) |
| Fireplace with electronic ignition (no pilot until you switch it on) | Only if it has a battery backup | Its igniter needs electricity, from the mains or a battery; some makers' fireplaces carry a battery pack that lights the pilot in a power cut (Heatilator battery backup) |
| Tank water heater with a standing pilot | Yes | Its gas control can run on a thermopile heated by the pilot (Resideo WT8840) |
| Power-vent or tankless water heater (fan on top, or a cord or plug) | Assume no | It has electric parts it needs to fire |
| Gas range top burners | Yes, lit with a match | The spark igniter needs power, but the burners can be lit by hand (GE outage) |
| Gas oven with a glow-bar igniter | No | GE says the igniter and gas valve need power to open (GE outage) |
| Gas furnace with an inducer fan and hot-surface or spark igniter | No | It needs 115–120 V to run, and lights itself (Goodman IO-359J, Lennox EL297UHV) |
| Gas boiler | Assume no | See the hydronic boiler device: most have a pump and controls on mains power |

Energir (Quebec's gas utility) notes that a gas fireplace can serve as stand-alone extra heat with no electrical hook-up (Energir fireplace). With a standing pilot, it is the gas appliance most likely to keep one room warm through a long power cut, for as long as the gas keeps flowing.

## How a standing pilot works with no power

A standing pilot is a small flame that burns all the time. On a millivolt fireplace, the pilot heats two sensors. The thermocouple makes enough electricity to hold the gas valve open, which is why you hold the knob in while the pilot warms up. The thermopile makes the power for the on/off switch, remote or thermostat. Because the pilot makes its own power, the fireplace runs in a power cut, but the blower doesn't (Travis 864 ST). The Travis 864 ST is rated at up to 37,500 Btu/h (about 11 kW) input (Travis 864 ST), which is real heat for a room.

Standing-pilot tank water heaters use the same idea: Resideo's WT8840 water-heater gas control is powered by a thermopile heated by the standing pilot (Resideo WT8840). With no power and the pilot lit, it keeps making hot water.

## How to tell which you have

- **A small flame burning when the main burner is off** (look through the glass or behind the lower grille or access cover): standing pilot.
- **A valve knob marked OFF, PILOT and ON, with a push-button igniter beside it:** a millivolt valve lit with a piezo igniter (Travis 864 ST).
- **Thin two-wire cable to a wall switch, and no plug:** the switch runs on thermopile power.
- **No pilot until you press the switch, a power cord or plug, or a battery holder:** electronic ignition. Some newer fireplaces carry a battery backup that lights them in a power cut; read the manual or the label.
- **Rating plate:** it names the gas (natural gas or propane), the input and the vent type. Direct vent and B-vent appliances send exhaust outside. Vent-free (also called ventless or unvented) appliances send it into the room (see below). See [Reading heater labels](#guides/reference_heater_labels).
- **Wall heaters:** check a gas wall furnace or room heater the same way. One with a standing pilot, a millivolt valve and no cord or plug works on the same principle.

## Furnaces and boilers

A modern forced-air furnace needs 115–120 V for its inducer fan, igniter, control board and blower (Goodman IO-359J; Lennox EL297UHV). It lights itself, and both makers say never to light the burner by hand (Goodman IO-359J; Lennox EL297UHV). With no power it is cold metal. To run one from a generator or inverter, see [Furnace backup power](#guides/build_furnace_backup_power). Hot-water boilers are covered on the hydronic boiler device.

## Gas ranges and ovens

GE says to light a top burner in an outage by holding a lit match to it and turning the knob to LO, with care, and to keep every burner either lit or off, because a knob at LITE or a power setting lets gas flow (GE outage). The oven is different: its glow-bar igniter and gas valve need power to open, so it can't be lit with a match, and an oven that was on when the power went shuts off with no gas flowing (GE outage).

**The oven and top burners are never room heaters.** The propane industry's safety guide says never to use a gas oven or range-top burners for heating (PERC safety guide). They run with no flue, straight into the kitchen. Cook, then turn them off, with a window open a crack while the burner is lit. See [Cooking indoors](#guides/reference_cooking_indoors).

## Vent-free gas logs and heaters

Vent-free (unvented, ventless) fireplaces, logs and room heaters release their combustion products straight into the room (CPSC glass 2013; Regency ventless). They are sold in the US but are not approved for use in Canada, and NRCan's guide says to avoid them in Canadian housing (NRCan gas fireplaces); Regency says indoor ventless gas fireplaces can't be sold in Canada (Regency ventless). A Canadian house is therefore more likely to have a direct-vent or B-vent fireplace; read the label of any unit that looks vent-free. If you find a vent-free unit:
- It has an oxygen-depletion sensor that shuts it off if oxygen gets too low (Regency ventless). That is not a CO alarm. Fit a battery CO alarm in the room.
- Regency suggests running one no more than 2 to 3 hours at a time (Regency ventless). Follow the maker's limits on its label.
- It puts a lot of water vapour into the room, which means damp and mould (Regency ventless). See [Condensation and damp](#guides/reference_condensation).
- Keep a window open a crack while it burns, and never run it in a bedroom or while anyone sleeps.

## Before you rely on any of these

- Every gas flame makes carbon monoxide. Fit battery CO alarms, check vents after every snowfall, and read [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).
- Fireplace glass gets very hot: the US CPSC says the glass front can reach 500 °F or even 1,000 °F, about 260 to 540 °C (CPSC glass blog 2014). The US (ANSI) standard was due to require, from January 2015, a protective barrier on vented gas fireplaces whose glass front passes 172 °F (about 78 °C) (CPSC glass 2013). Older fireplaces may have none. If the screen is missing, put a guard in front that keeps hands off the glass and doesn't get hot enough to burn itself (CPSC glass 2013), especially with children around.
- If the gas supply itself fails, pilots go out. Close every appliance's valve before the gas comes back: see [Gas safety](#guides/safety_natural_gas). When gas is restored, Manitoba Hydro says you may need to relight the pilots on your furnace and water heater yourself, and to call it if you don't know how (Manitoba Hydro winter); Enbridge Gas tells its customers to leave relighting to a technician (Enbridge outage).
- Clear snow from the gas meter by hand, and don't kick or hit it to break ice (BC gas brochure).
